claim: A novel variant of the SARS-CoV-2 virus carrying a point mutation in the Spike protein (D614G) has recently emerged and rapidly surpassed others in prevalence.
source: A novel variant of the SARS-CoV-2 virus carrying a point mutation in the Spike protein (D614G) has recently emerged and rapidly surpassed others in prevalence.
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic surveillance data from GISAID showing temporal increase in G614 prevalence.

claim: The Spike D614G mutation is in linkage disequilibrium with an ORF1b protein variant (P314L).
source: This mutation is in linkage disequilibrium with an ORF1b protein variant (P314L), making it difficult to discern the functional significance of the Spike D614G mutation from population genetics alone.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bhattacharyya et al., 2020 and genomic analysis.

claim: Lentiviral particles pseudotyped with Spike D614G are more effective at transducing cells than ones pseudotyped with wild-type Spike.
source: Using multiple human cell lines, including human lung epithelial cells, we found that the lentiviral particles pseudotyped with Spike D614G are more effective at transducing cells than ones pseudotyped with wild-type Spike.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from flow cytometry measurements of transduced cells.

claim: The increased transduction with Spike D614G ranged from 1.3- to 2.4-fold in Caco-2 and Calu-3 cells expressing endogenous ACE2.
source: The increased transduction with Spike D614G ranged from 1.3- to 2.4-fold in Caco-2 and Calu-3 cells expressing endogenous ACE2 and from 1.5- to 7.7-fold in A549ACE2 and Huh7.5ACE2 overexpressing ACE2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The increased transduction with Spike D614G ranged from 1.5- to 7.7-fold in A549ACE2 and Huh7.5ACE2 overexpressing ACE2.
source: The increased transduction with Spike D614G ranged from 1.3- to 2.4-fold in Caco-2 and Calu-3 cells expressing endogenous ACE2 and from 1.5- to 7.7-fold in A549ACE2 and Huh7.5ACE2 overexpressing ACE2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Trans-complementation of SARS-CoV-2 virus with Spike D614G showed an increased infectivity in human cells.
source: Furthermore, trans-complementation of SARS-CoV-2 virus with Spike D614G showed an increased infectivity in human cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the trans-complementation assay shown in Figure 4.

claim: There is minimal difference in ACE2 receptor binding between the D614 and G614 Spike variants.
source: Although there is minimal difference in ACE2 receptor binding between the D614 and G614 Spike variants, the G614 variant is more resistant to proteolytic cleavage, suggesting a possible mechanism for the increased transduction.
evidence: This is supported by bio-layer interferometry data shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: The G614 variant is more resistant to proteolytic cleavage.
source: Although there is minimal difference in ACE2 receptor binding between the D614 and G614 Spike variants, the G614 variant is more resistant to proteolytic cleavage, suggesting a possible mechanism for the increased transduction.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data showing reduced cleavage of G614 Spike in Figure 3.

claim: The Spike D614G variant is a defining feature of the most prevalent clade (A2a) of SARS-CoV-2 genomes worldwide.
source: This Spike variant is a defining feature of the most prevalent clade (A2a) of SARS-CoV-2 genomes worldwide (Bhattacharyya et al., 2020; Hadfield et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to phylogenomic studies.

claim: Approximately 72% of 22,103 SARS-CoV-2 genomes surveyed from GISAID in early June 2020 contained the G614 variant.
source: We found that ~72% of 22,103 SARS-CoV-2 genomes that we surveyed from the GISAID public repository in early June 2020 contained the G614 variant (Shu and McCauley, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of genomic data from GISAID.

claim: There is a significant positive correlation between the prevalence of G614 in a country with its case-fatality rate (rp = 0.29, p=0.04).
source: Using a ~10-fold larger dataset, we found a smaller yet significant positive correlation between the prevalence of G614 in a country with its case-fatality rate (rp = 0.29, p=0.04) (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of GISAID genomic data and Johns Hopkins case-fatality rate data.

claim: In COVID-19 patients there is a ~3-fold increase in viral RNA during quantitative PCR (qPCR) testing for those patients with the G614 variant.
source: Recently, two separate groups at the University of Sheffield and at the University of Washington have found that in COVID-19 patients there is a ~3-fold increase in viral RNA during quantitative PCR (qPCR) testing for those patients with the G614 variant (Korber et al., 2020; Wagner et al., 2020; Figure 1c,d).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies and reanalysis of their data.

claim: The difference in qPCR amplification (ΔΔCt) between G614 and D614 variants is remarkably consistent (1.6 Ct for Sheffield, 1.8 Ct for Washington).
source: However, the difference in amplification (ΔΔCt) between G614 and D614 variants is remarkably consistent (1.6 Ct for Sheffield, 1.8 Ct for Washington), suggesting that this may be due to a biological difference between COVID-19 patients with specific Spike variants (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by reanalysis of published qPCR data from two independent studies.

claim: S-virus is much more efficient at transducing human cell lines when the human ACE2 receptor is overexpressed.
source: Others have observed increased S-virus transduction in cells that overexpress the ACE2 receptor (Li et al., 2003; Moore et al., 2004); we also found that S-virus is much more efficient at transducing human cell lines when the human ACE2 receptor is overexpressed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Lentivirus lacking an attachment protein resulted in negligible transduction.
source: Lentivirus lacking an attachment protein resulted in negligible transduction (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental flow cytometry data serving as a negative control.

claim: With the G614 Spike variant, the increase in viral transduction over the D614 variant ranged from 1.4- to 1.9-fold for Calu-3.
source: With the G614 Spike variant, the increase in viral transduction over the D614 variant ranged from 1.4- to 1.9-fold for Calu-3, 1.3- to 2.4-fold for Caco-2 colon, 1.8- to 4.6-fold for A549ACE2 lung, and 1.5- to 7.7-fold for Huh7.5ACE2 liver, depending on the specific dose of S-virus (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental flow cytometry data.

claim: With the G614 Spike variant, the increase in viral transduction over the D614 variant ranged from 1.3- to 2.4-fold for Caco-2 colon.
source: With the G614 Spike variant, the increase in viral transduction over the D614 variant ranged from 1.4- to 1.9-fold for Calu-3, 1.3- to 2.4-fold for Caco-2 colon, 1.8- to 4.6-fold for A549ACE2 lung, and 1.5- to 7.7-fold for Huh7.5ACE2 liver, depending on the specific dose of S-virus (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental flow cytometry data.

claim: With the G614 Spike variant, the increase in viral transduction over the D614 variant ranged from 1.8- to 4.6-fold for A549ACE2 lung.
source: With the G614 Spike variant, the increase in viral transduction over the D614 variant ranged from 1.4- to 1.9-fold for Calu-3, 1.3- to 2.4-fold for Caco-2 colon, 1.8- to 4.6-fold for A549ACE2 lung, and 1.5- to 7.7-fold for Huh7.5ACE2 liver, depending on the specific dose of S-virus (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental flow cytometry data.

claim: With the G614 Spike variant, the increase in viral transduction over the D614 variant ranged from 1.5- to 7.7-fold for Huh7.5ACE2 liver.
source: With the G614 Spike variant, the increase in viral transduction over the D614 variant ranged from 1.4- to 1.9-fold for Calu-3, 1.3- to 2.4-fold for Caco-2 colon, 1.8- to 4.6-fold for A549ACE2 lung, and 1.5- to 7.7-fold for Huh7.5ACE2 liver, depending on the specific dose of S-virus (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental flow cytometry data.

claim: There was only a small difference between D614- and G614-pseudotyped viruses in viral RNA content (average of 7% higher viral titer for D614).
source: We observed only a small difference between D614- and G614-pseudotyped viruses using two independent primer sets (average of 7% higher viral titer for D614), which may result in a slight underestimation of the increase in transduction efficacy of the G614-pseudotyped virus (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data measuring viral RNA content.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein has both a receptor-binding domain and a hydrophobic fusion polypeptide that is used after binding the receptor to fuse the viral and host cell membranes.
source: Like SARS-CoV-1, the SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein has both a receptor-binding domain and a hydrophobic fusion polypeptide that is used after binding the receptor (e.g. ACE2) to fuse the viral and host cell membranes (Heald-Sargent and Gallagher, 2012; Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and established knowledge of coronavirus biology.

claim: Similar binding profiles of soluble D614 and G614 Spike S1 subunit to immobilized hACE2 were observed.
source: We observed similar binding profiles of soluble D614 and G614 Spike S1 subunit to immobilized hACE2 (Figure 3b,c).
evidence: This is supported by bio-layer interferometry experimental data.

claim: Binding of Spike S1 to ACE2 was best represented by a 2:1 heterogeneous binding model with KD1 = 8.45 nM and KD2 = 127 nM for D614 variant.
source: Binding was best represented by a 2:1 heterogeneous binding model, which reports two dissociation constants (KD): KD1 = 8.45 nM and KD2 = 127 nM for D614 variant, and KD1 = 18.0 nM and KD2 = 92.7 nM for G614 variant (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by bio-layer interferometry data and kinetic modeling.

claim: Binding of Spike S1 to ACE2 was best represented by a 2:1 heterogeneous binding model with KD1 = 18.0 nM and KD2 = 92.7 nM for G614 variant.
source: Binding was best represented by a 2:1 heterogeneous binding model, which reports two dissociation constants (KD): KD1 = 8.45 nM and KD2 = 127 nM for D614 variant, and KD1 = 18.0 nM and KD2 = 92.7 nM for G614 variant (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by bio-layer interferometry data and kinetic modeling.

claim: KD1 is consistent with previously published binding affinities of the Spike D614–ACE2 interaction.
source: KD1 is consistent with previously published binding affinities of the Spike D614–ACE2 interaction (Walls et al., 2020; Yi et al., 2020) and is similar for the Spike G614 variant.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with cited literature values.

claim: The observed transduction phenotype is independent of Spike S1 subunit affinity for the ACE2 receptor.
source: This suggests our observed transduction phenotype is independent of Spike S1 subunit affinity for the ACE2 receptor.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar binding affinities measured for D614 and G614 variants.

claim: Spike must first be cleaved into S1 and S2 fragments, which exposes another cleavage site.
source: It is thought that Spike must first be cleaved into S1 and S2 fragments, which exposes another cleavage site (Bestle et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on SARS-CoV-2 entry mechanisms.

claim: The second cleavage event (creating the S2' fragment) is thought to enable membrane fusion with the host cell.
source: The second cleavage event (creating the S2' fragment) is thought to enable membrane fusion with the host cell.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of coronavirus entry mechanisms.

claim: The G614 variant is approximately 2.5 fold more resistant to cleavage in the host cell than the D614 variant in cells expressing Spike by transient transfection.
source: We found that the G614 variant is ~2.5 fold more resistant to cleavage in the host cell than the D614 variant in cells expressing Spike by transient transfection (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is supported by western blot quantification data.

claim: Virions with the G614 variant have less Spike cleavage compared to the D614 variant (approximately 1.4-fold).
source: We found that virions with the G614 variant have less Spike cleavage compared to the D614 variant (~1.4-fold) (Figure 3i).
evidence: This is supported by western blot quantification of pseudotyped lentiviral particles.

claim: The increased transduction observed with G614 S-virus may be due to the greater fraction of uncleaved G614 Spike, which perhaps enable each newly-assembled virion to include more receptor-binding-capable Spike protein.
source: This suggests that the increased transduction observed with G614 S-virus (Figure 2d) may be due to the greater fraction of uncleaved G614 Spike, which perhaps enable each newly-assembled virion to include more receptor-binding-capable Spike protein.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism inferred from the cleavage data.

claim: There was no significant difference between Spike D614 and Spike G614 incorporation into pseudotyped lentiviral particles.
source: We found no significant difference between Spike D614 and Spike G614 incorporation into pseudotyped lentiviral particles.
evidence: This is supported by western blot quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There are presently 174 COVID-19 vaccine candidates in preclinical development and 63 vaccine candidates in patient-enrolling clinical trials.
source: According to the World Health Organization, there are presently 174 COVID-19 vaccine candidates in preclinical development and 63 vaccine candidates in patient-enrolling clinical trials (https://www.who.int/publications/m/item/draft-landscape-of-covid-19-candidate-vaccines, accessed on January 26, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to WHO data.

claim: Many COVID-19 vaccine candidates utilize Spike sequences (RNA or DNA) or peptides and were developed prior to the emergence of the G614 variant.
source: Despite the tremendous diversity of vaccine formulations and delivery methods, many of them utilize Spike sequences (RNA or DNA) or peptides and were developed prior to the emergence of the G614 variant.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of vaccine development timelines and approaches.

claim: The G614 variant can alter predicted MHC binding.
source: Using epitope prediction for common HLA alleles (Andreatta and Nielsen, 2016), we found that the G614 variant can alter predicted MHC binding ( Figure 3-figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by computational epitope prediction data.

claim: The predicted binding for one high-affinity epitope decreased by nearly fourfold (58 nM for D614 versus 221 nM for G614 with HLA-A*02:01).
source: For example, the predicted binding for one high-affinity epitope decreased by nearly fourfold (58 nM for D614 versus 221 nM for G614 with HLA-A*02:01).
evidence: This is supported by computational epitope prediction data.

claim: Several vaccines use only portions of Spike.
source: Although full-length Spike protein likely can produce many immunogenic peptides, several vaccines use only portions of Spike (Lurie et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2020) and thus it may be better to adapt vaccine efforts to the D614 variant given its global spread.
evidence: This is supported by citations to vaccine development literature.

claim: Isolates from patient samples that carry the Spike variant also carry a linked mutation in ORF1b.
source: Isolates from patient samples that carry the Spike variant also carry a linked mutation in ORF1b, which makes it challenging to perform this experiment in an isogenic fashion.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis showing linkage disequilibrium.

claim: Most cell lines require ACE2 overexpression for efficient SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: In lieu of a reverse genetics system to generate a SARS-CoV-2 variant and building on the observation by several groups that most cell lines require ACE2 overexpression for efficient SARS-CoV-2 infection (Hoffmann et al., 2020; Ou et al., 2020; Shang et al., 2020; Ziegler et al., 2020), we developed a novel trans-complementation assay in which we co-transfect either D614 or G614 Spike along with human ACE2 into HEK293T cells (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Significant increases in infection with SARS-CoV-2 complemented with Spike G614 were found at all time points and all MOIs.
source: We found significant increases in infection with SARS-CoV-2 complemented with Spike G614 at all time points and all MOIs (Figure 4c,d).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data from the trans-complementation assay.

claim: Infected HEK293T cells without any prior transfection resulted in minimal SARS-CoV-2 infection (<1% in most cases).
source: As a negative control, infected HEK293T cells without any prior transfection resulted in minimal SARS-CoV-2 infection (<1% in most cases).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data serving as a negative control.

claim: Introduction of just the Spike D614G point mutation increases infection using intact (replication-competent) SARS-CoV-2 virus.
source: Using the trans-complementation assay, we have shown that introduction of just the Spike D614G point mutation increases infection using intact (replication-competent) SARS-CoV-2 virus.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the trans-complementation assay.

claim: The D614G mutation in the SARS-CoV-2 Spike glycoprotein increases the efficiency of cellular entry for the virus across a broad range of human cell types, including cells from lung, liver, and colon.
source: In summary, we have demonstrated that the recent and now-dominant mutation in the SARS-CoV-2 Spike glycoprotein D614G increases the efficiency of cellular entry for the virus across a broad range of human cell types, including cells from lung, liver, and colon.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from multiple cell lines.

claim: Increased entry efficiency was shown using both a pseudotyped lentiviral model system and a replication-competent SARS-CoV-2 virus.
source: We showed increased entry efficiency using both a pseudotyped lentiviral model system and a replication-competent SARS-CoV-2 virus.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from both systems.

claim: The concordance between the pseudotyped lentiviral system and SARS-CoV-2 virus suggests that changes in Spike protein are well represented using the pseudovirus.
source: Given the concordance between the pseudotyped lentiviral system and SARS-CoV-2 virus, this suggests that changes in Spike protein are well represented using the pseudovirus, which should enable a much broader group of laboratories to use and study Spike variants.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar results obtained with both systems.

claim: G614 Spike is more resistant to proteolytic cleavage during production of the protein in host cells as well as on pseudotyped lentiviral particles.
source: We also found that G614 Spike is more resistant to proteolytic cleavage during production of the protein in host cells as well as on pseudotyped lentiviral particles, suggesting that replicated virus produced in human cells may be more infectious due to a greater proportion of functional (uncleaved with receptor-binding domain) Spike protein per virion.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data.

claim: Replicated virus produced in human cells may be more infectious due to a greater proportion of functional (uncleaved with receptor-binding domain) Spike protein per virion.
source: We also found that G614 Spike is more resistant to proteolytic cleavage during production of the protein in host cells as well as on pseudotyped lentiviral particles, suggesting that replicated virus produced in human cells may be more infectious due to a greater proportion of functional (uncleaved with receptor-binding domain) Spike protein per virion.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism inferred from the cleavage data.

claim: A recent study with Spike-pseudotyped murine leukemia virus observed a difference in Spike incorporation into lentiviral particles with the G614 variant.
source: In contrast to a recent study with Spike-pseudotyped murine leukemia virus (Zhang et al., 2020), we did not observe a difference in Spike incorporation into lentiviral particles with the G614 variant as compared to the D614 variant, which is consistent with observations by other groups (Ozono et al., 2020; Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: The current study did not observe a difference in Spike incorporation into lentiviral particles with the G614 variant as compared to the D614 variant, which is consistent with observations by other groups.
source: In contrast to a recent study with Spike-pseudotyped murine leukemia virus (Zhang et al., 2020), we did not observe a difference in Spike incorporation into lentiviral particles with the G614 variant as compared to the D614 variant, which is consistent with observations by other groups (Ozono et al., 2020; Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to other studies.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 Spike is proteolytically processed primarily by furin.
source: It is now well established that SARS-CoV-2 Spike is proteolytically processed primarily by furin; however, new reports suggest that G614 maybe also processed by elastase-2 (Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of SARS-CoV-2 biology.

claim: New reports suggest that G614 may also be processed by elastase-2.
source: It is now well established that SARS-CoV-2 Spike is proteolytically processed primarily by furin; however, new reports suggest that G614 maybe also processed by elastase-2 (Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hu et al., 2020.

claim: Using bio-layer interferometry with purified SARS-CoV-2 Spike S1 fragment monomers and ACE2 proteins, no significant difference in binding kinetics with the ACE2 receptor resulting from the D614G mutation was found.
source: Using bio-layer interferometry with purified SARS-CoV-2 Spike S1 fragment monomers and ACE2 proteins, we found no significant difference in binding kinetics with the ACE2 receptor resulting from the D614G mutation.
evidence: This is supported by bio-layer interferometry data.

claim: With purified Spike full-length trimers, the G614 mutation shifts the Spike protein conformation to an ACE2-binding competent state.
source: Yurkovetskiy and colleagues reported that, with purified Spike full-length trimers, the G614 mutation shifts the Spike protein conformation to an ACE2-binding competent state (Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020), suggesting that Spike full-length trimers behave differently than the Spike S1 monomers that we investigated in this study.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020.

claim: Spike full-length trimers behave differently than the Spike S1 monomers.
source: Yurkovetskiy and colleagues reported that, with purified Spike full-length trimers, the G614 mutation shifts the Spike protein conformation to an ACE2-binding competent state (Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020), suggesting that Spike full-length trimers behave differently than the Spike S1 monomers that we investigated in this study.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing results with different protein forms.

claim: Several other groups have reported that the D614G results in increased viral fitness and infection efficiency.
source: Several other groups have also reported that the D614G results in increased viral fitness and infection efficiency (Hu et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Ozono et al., 2020; Plante et al., 2020; Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Most studies reporting increased viral fitness with D614G utilized Spike-pseudotyped viral particles to demonstrate this finding.
source: Most of them utilized Spike-pseudotyped viral particles to demonstrate this finding.
evidence: This is based on review of cited literature.

claim: The common consensus is that Spike G614 mutation increases viral fitness and infectivity.
source: While the common consensus is that Spike G614 mutation increases viral fitness and infectivity, the mechanism by which it occurs varies among these studies.
evidence: This is based on review of multiple studies.

claim: The mechanism by which the G614 mutation increases viral fitness varies among studies.
source: While the common consensus is that Spike G614 mutation increases viral fitness and infectivity, the mechanism by which it occurs varies among these studies.
evidence: This is based on review of multiple studies showing different proposed mechanisms.

claim: Technical differences in protocols used to generate Spike-pseudotyped viral particles can explain discrepancies between studies regarding proteolytic processing and incorporation of Spike.
source: This can be explained, at least in part, by the technical differences in the protocols used to generate the Spike-pseudotyped viral particles.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing methodological differences across studies.

claim: Studies use a wide variety of pseudoviral systems, such as murine leukemia virus, mouse sarcoma virus, and lentivirus.
source: For example, the studies use a wide variety of pseudoviral systems, such as murine leukemia virus (Zhang et al., 2020), mouse sarcoma virus (Jiang et al., 2020), and lentivirus (our study and Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on review of cited literature.

claim: Two studies that utilized isogenic SARS-CoV-2 D614 and G614 variants found no difference in Spike protein cleavage and incorporation into viral particles.
source: Two studies that utilized isogenic SARS-CoV-2 D614 and G614 variants found no difference in Spike protein cleavage and incorporation into viral particles (Hou et al., 2020; Plante et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to these studies.

claim: Differences in Spike biology between isogenic pseudoviruses and SARS-CoV-2 viruses may be due to differences in Spike protein trimer assembly and presentation, as well as the absence/presence of additional SARS-CoV-2 proteins.
source: The differences in Spike biology between isogenic pseudoviruses and SARS-CoV-2 viruses may be due to differences in Spike protein trimer assembly and presentation, as well as the absence/presence of additional SARS-CoV-2 proteins.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential causes of observed differences.

claim: There is emerging consensus that G614 results in faster viral spread.
source: Despite the emerging consensus the G614 results in faster viral spread (Korber et al., 2020), it is still uncertain whether this will have a clinical impact on COVID-19 disease progression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Korber et al., 2020.

claim: It is still uncertain whether G614 will have a clinical impact on COVID-19 disease progression.
source: Despite the emerging consensus the G614 results in faster viral spread (Korber et al., 2020), it is still uncertain whether this will have a clinical impact on COVID-19 disease progression.
evidence: This is based on review of available clinical data.

claim: Two studies that examined potential differences in clinical severity or hospitalization rates did not see a correlation with Spike mutation status.
source: Two studies that have examined potential differences in clinical severity or hospitalization rates did not see a correlation with Spike mutation status (Korber et al., 2020; Wagner et al., 2020), although one study found a small but not significant enrichment of G614 mutations among intensive care unit patients (Korber et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: One study found a small but not significant enrichment of G614 mutations among intensive care unit patients.
source: Two studies that have examined potential differences in clinical severity or hospitalization rates did not see a correlation with Spike mutation status (Korber et al., 2020; Wagner et al., 2020), although one study found a small but not significant enrichment of G614 mutations among intensive care unit patients (Korber et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Korber et al., 2020.

claim: The G614 variant and other recent variants merit careful consideration by biomedical researchers working on candidate therapies and vaccines.
source: Given its rapid rise in human isolates and enhanced transduction across a broad spectrum of human cell types, the G614 variant and other recent variants merit careful consideration by biomedical researchers working on candidate therapies, such as those to modulate cellular proteases, and on vaccines that deliver Spike D614 nucleic acids or peptides.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.

claim: Caco-2 and Calu-3 cells express endogenous angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2).
source: Caco-2 and Calu-3 cells express endogenous angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) (Ren et al., 2006); for A549 and Huh7.5, we overexpressed ACE2 using a lentiviral construct (A549ACE2, Huh7.5ACE2).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ren et al., 2006.

claim: For A549 and Huh7.5 cells, ACE2 was overexpressed using a lentiviral construct.
source: Caco-2 and Calu-3 cells express endogenous angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) (Ren et al., 2006); for A549 and Huh7.5, we overexpressed ACE2 using a lentiviral construct (A549ACE2, Huh7.5ACE2).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental methods described.

claim: The first sequenced SARS-CoV-2 isolate (GenBank accession MN908947.3) contained an aspartic acid at position 614 of the Spike protein.
source: The first sequenced SARS-CoV-2 isolate (GenBank accession MN908947.3) and the majority of viral sequences acquired in January and February 2020 contained an aspartic acid at position 614 of the Spike protein (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by reference to the GenBank sequence and genomic data.

claim: The majority of viral sequences acquired in January and February 2020 contained an aspartic acid at position 614 of the Spike protein.
source: The first sequenced SARS-CoV-2 isolate (GenBank accession MN908947.3) and the majority of viral sequences acquired in January and February 2020 contained an aspartic acid at position 614 of the Spike protein (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by genomic surveillance data.

claim: Beginning in February 2020, an increasing number of SARS-CoV-2 variants with glycine at position 614 of the Spike protein were identified.
source: Beginning in February 2020, an increasing number of SARS-CoV-2 variants with glycine at position 614 of the Spike protein were identified.
evidence: This is supported by genomic surveillance data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Cardozo and colleagues reported a correlation between the prevalence of the G614 variant and the case-fatality rate in individual localities using viral genomes available through early April 2020.
source: Previously, Cardozo and colleagues reported a correlation between the prevalence of the G614 variant and the case-fatality rate in individual localities using viral genomes available through early April 2020 (Becerra-Flores and Cardozo, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Becerra-Flores and Cardozo, 2020.

claim: Some groups have proposed that the D614G variant may confer increased transmissibility leading to positive selection.
source: Using phylogenomic data, several groups have proposed that the D614G variant may confer increased transmissibility leading to positive selection (Bhattacharyya et al., 2020), while others have claimed that currently available evidence does not support positive selection (Dorp et al., 2020; Korber et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bhattacharyya et al., 2020.

claim: Some groups have claimed that currently available evidence does not support positive selection of the D614G variant.
source: Using phylogenomic data, several groups have proposed that the D614G variant may confer increased transmissibility leading to positive selection (Bhattacharyya et al., 2020), while others have claimed that currently available evidence does not support positive selection (Dorp et al., 2020; Korber et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dorp et al., 2020 and Korber et al., 2020.

claim: Neutralizing antibodies that target the receptor-binding domain seem largely unaffected in potency by the D614G variant.
source: For example, neutralizing antibodies that target the receptor-binding domain seem largely unaffected in potency, but it remains to be seen whether the D614G variant alters neutralization sensitivity to other classes of anti-Spike antibodies (Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020.

claim: It remains to be seen whether the D614G variant alters neutralization sensitivity to other classes of anti-Spike antibodies.
source: For example, neutralizing antibodies that target the receptor-binding domain seem largely unaffected in potency, but it remains to be seen whether the D614G variant alters neutralization sensitivity to other classes of anti-Spike antibodies (Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculation about future research needs.
